summary.title: XOR
summary.one_liner: XOR (exclusive or) is a bit operation that means "different" or "addition mod 2", and it is useful for bitwise flipping, simple encryption, and reversible drawing.
takeaways: XOR outputs 1 when its two inputs differ, and equals addition mod 2 or the 'invert b if a is true' operation.
XOR is commutative, associative, has 0 as identity, and any value XORed with itself is 0, so repeated terms cancel.
Applied bitwise to integers, XOR flips exactly the bits named by a control value; e.g. XOR with 32 switches ASCII letter case.
XOR is used in simple stream-cipher style encryption because encrypting and decrypting are the same operation and it is cheap in hardware.
In 1980s graphics, XOR drawing lets you draw and undraw sprites or lines without storing the background, since drawing twice restores the original pixels.
summary.summary: Simon Tatham explains the XOR operator from first principles, starting with its truth table and several equivalent intuitions: inequality, conditional inversion, and parity (addition mod 2). He covers algebraic laws such as commutativity, associativity, identity and self-inverse, then extends them bitwise to whole integers with worked binary and hex examples. The article then shows applications: a simple XOR keystream encryption scheme and reversible XOR-based drawing in 1980s home computer graphics. The piece is an essay-style lecture text with truth tables and examples rather than a code tutorial.
